newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico watchers downplay monetary concern.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico watchers downplay monetary concern.

text.p: The size of Mexico's monetary base has again become an issue on financial markets, but Mexican central bank watchers for the most part downplayed the concerns on Friday.
They agreed Banco de Mexico has been for the main part trying to meet a stronger-than-expected demand for cash and in the process has pushed up the size of the monetary base past expectations.
Analysts said that, if anything, monetary policy has remained tight, with high nominal interest rates coupled to low inflation to give high real interest rates and a strong exchange rate.
"I think that, if anything, it (the rising monetary base) is a sign demand may be a little stronger than projected," Valores Finamex economist Ann Ginsburg said.

The central bank started in January to publish monetary base forecasts for each day of the year, publishing the expected data based on historic demand patterns. The central bank supplies markets with cash based on estimated demand.
The monetary base is made up mainly of coins and bills in circulation.
While monetary base growth followed the central bank forecasts reasonably closely during the first part of the year, it began to decouple more sharply in mid-March, analysts said.
"I just don't see it (monetary base growth) as a concern, while interest rates are at the higher end of historical levels," HSBC James Capel economist Gray Newman said.

Some observers have become concerned that, prior to key mid-term elections in July, the central bank could be priming the monetary pump -- such as was done before the 1994 presidential election -- and in the process fuel inflation.

But the central bank says it is keeping to a neutral monetary stance, trying to satisfy demand without creating inflationary pressures. Its officials say the greater demand could be tied to better-than-forecast growth rather than demand tied to inflationary pressures.
"It could be very logical that it (base growth) is tied to real demand and not for an inflationary demand for money," said Mexico City economist Jonathan Heath.
"But the Banco de Mexico is entering into dangerous territory. They could be playing with (inflationary ) expectations," he said.
Analysts said any sustained overshooting of the monetary base targets would quickly show up in the exchange rate.
Heath said central bank officials have signalled they are concerned about the overshooting of the monetary base and are expected to take measures to bring it closer to the outlined targets.
Analysts said the central bank is concerned that neither interest rates nor the exchange rate strengthen too sharply, which could then bring about a steeper correction.
The central bank has struggled to mop up dollars flowing into Mexico from the bank's option scheme, government debt issues and from state oil and gas company Petroleos Mexicanos.
